_about: Papers checked in the systematic screening that began on 22 Nov 2026 (method on about.html#selection). Rendered to checked.html by tools/build.py. Outcomes: clean = no error found; nomaterial = no material error found (checked or rerun); reviewed = method reviewed but data not rerun, no material error found; inprint = already corrected or challenged in print by others; withauthors = finding sent to the authors (count only until they reply or three weeks pass; then add the paper by name, outcome 'flagged', with a link to its register entry); inprogress = check not finished. side: mainstream or questioning (papers questioning mainstream climate findings). 'datasets' and 'code' lists work the same way (no side); flagged datasets and code that are public come automatically from the register (register_rows.json areas 'Observing data' and 'Code' with a 'Real…' verdict, plus custom entries).

papers.topic: Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds (Google flood forecasting vs GloFAS)
papers.note: Already challenged in print: Li, Razavi, Maier, Hrachowitz et al. 2026, Journal of Hydrology X 30, 100215 (doi:10.1016/j.hydroa.2026.100215) — event thresholds taken from modelled rather than observed flows, a ±2-day hit window, no testing beyond 10-year events, high false-alarm and miss rates, and a single global benchmark. We did not repeat that work.

papers.cite: Schöngart et al. 2025, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: Contributions of high-income groups to warming and to heat and drought extremes
papers.note: Checked with the authors' Zenodo data (14860538): extra 1-in-100 heat events attributed to the top 10% and top 1% are 69% and 22% of the total, close to their 65% and 20% shares of attributed warming; the metric counts additional events, so it does not have the near-zero-baseline problem of probability ratios.

papers.cite: Waidelich et al. 2024, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: Climate damage projections beyond annual temperature (10% of GDP at +3 °C)
papers.note: Reran the main regression (the Kotz et al. 2022 specification) from the authors' Zenodo files. The regional GDP panel contains implausible growth values (Uzbekistan 1996–99 at +37% to +61% per year in log terms; tenfold jumps in some Kenyan, Spanish and Malaysian regions), but dropping Uzbekistan or all |Δlog GDP| > 0.5 changes the temperature effect by under 0.1 percentage points. No material error found.

papers.topic: Climate warming is expanding dengue burden in the Americas and Asia (18% of cases attributed to past warming)
papers.note: Refitted the main Poisson fixed-effects model on the shareable part of the data (Zenodo; mostly Brazil) and added future temperatures as a placebo: the lead terms are near zero (−0.016 against +0.76 for the lagged response at 20–21 °C). One robustness model (4th-order polynomial) repeats the lag-1 term instead of lags 2 and 3; this affects only that check. No material error found.

papers.topic: Global scale assessment of urban precipitation anomalies (over 60% of cities wetter than their surroundings)
papers.note: The paper has no placebo test, so we ran one with IMERG V07 (2001–2020 mean) and 1,487 GHS-SMOD urban centres: 59.7% of cities are wetter than their outer rural ring (paper: 63%), against 46.1% for the same discs moved away from any city. The urban excess holds for inland (56% vs 45%) and coastal (68% vs 51%) cities separately. No material error found.

papers.topic: Impact of Amazonian deforestation on precipitation reverses between seasons (WRF 2000 vs 2020 forest cover, 2001–2022)
papers.note: The paper's error bars are the standard error across spatially correlated grid cells, and there is no ensemble to measure chaotic model noise. Using the authors' figshare output we reproduced every buffer mean exactly (e.g. wet season +5.76 mm/month at 0 km, −0.28 at 60 km; dry season −1.55 at 40 km), then recomputed the uncertainty from the 22 independent yearly run pairs, which include the model's chaotic noise. The year-based errors are similar to or smaller than the published ones, and the sign of each effect is stable across years (e.g. the 60 km wet-season decrease: p = 0.008, 17 of 22 years negative). No material error found.

papers.topic: The enduring world forest carbon sink (3.6 / 3.6 / 3.5 Pg C per year by decade)
papers.note: Recomputed the 1990s-to-2010s biome changes and their uncertainties from Table 1 and the USDA data archive (RDS-2023-0051), treating decades as independent as the paper's own trend test does. The global sink result is unaffected. No material error found.

papers.cite: Wu et al. 2025, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: Decreasing dynamic predictability of global agricultural drought with warming climate
papers.note: Read the Supplementary Information and the archived figure code (Zenodo 12737359) and simulated the significance test applied to sliding-window skill (Mann–Kendall with trend-free pre-whitening, ensemble-agreement rule). The model inputs are not archived, so the headline could not be rerun. No material error found.

papers.cite: Chai et al. 2025, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: Constrained Earth system models show a stronger reduction in future Northern Hemisphere snowmelt water
papers.note: Checked the hierarchical emergent-constraint code against Bowman et al. (2018) and recomputed from the archived fields (GitHub): models' historical SWE is 1.55× the observations, and the raw future ensemble is 1.34× the constrained value, consistent with the paper. No material error found.

papers.cite: Wang et al. 2025, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: Dual impact of global urban overheating on mortality (cold benefit more than fourfold the heat cost)
papers.note: Recomputed from the archived city table (GitHub, 3,276 cities): the urban heat island's reduction in cold-related mortality is 4.6× its increase in heat-related mortality (paper: more than fourfold). The ratio follows from the standard temperature–mortality curves, in which moderate cold carries most attributable deaths. No material error found.

papers.topic: Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning (GenCast)
papers.note: Read the methods (arXiv v2): significance is tested with a stationary block bootstrap with automatic block length, so serial correlation between forecast dates is handled; each system is verified against its own analysis, and the look-ahead difference is stated. Forecast archives (WeatherBench 2) were not reachable from our workspace, so nothing was rerun.

papers.topic: End-to-end data-driven weather prediction (Aardvark Weather)
papers.note: Read the paper and the released code (GitHub aardvark-weather-public): training (to 2017), test (2018) and validation (2019) years are kept separate in the data loaders; station forecasts are tested on held-out years at stations seen in training, as the paper states. Gridded forecasts, including HRES and GFS, are verified against ERA5. Nothing was rerun.

papers.cite: Zeng et al. 2019, Nature Climate Change
papers.topic: A reversal in global terrestrial stilling and its implications for wind energy production
papers.note: Part of the post-2013 wind-speed increase in the station data was later traced to an undocumented change in how calm periods were encoded, which over-estimated average wind speeds in much of Asia and Europe (Dunn, Azorin-Molina, Menne, Zeng et al. 2022, Environ. Res. Commun. 4, 061003, doi:10.1088/2515-7620/ac770a). Instrument changes in the US network are the subject of our separate ASOS note (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.24357793).

code.topic: UTCI, WBGT, globe temperature and other heat-stress indices

code.note: Agree within their documented methods; pythermalcomfort and thermal_comfort could mention that their Stull formula is for sea level.

code.topic: Atmospheric radiation scheme (ECMWF IFS, ICON NWP physics)
code.note: Reproduces ECMWF's reference output exactly. Tested with gases set to zero, solver consistency, cloud and sun-angle limits, and doubled vertical resolution.

code.topic: Sea-ice column physics (used by CICE, E3SM and UFS)
code.note: Five-year runs with a seasonal cycle and energy and mass checks switched on: both thermodynamics schemes, three melt-pond schemes, heavy snow, rain on ice, very cold air and summers warm enough to melt all the ice. No conservation failures. The older thermodynamics scheme stops in some melt seasons unless its documented shortwave option is turned on; the documentation already says this.

Ran the 17 priority test cases: variances stayed positive, correlations within bounds, no NaNs. Where the model reports its column-water spurious source (5 of the 17 cases) it is at round-off level, and clipping of negative water is negligible in all cases. Results change at long time steps (20 minutes), but that is already documented in print (Wan et al. 2021, GMD; Santos et al. 2021, JAMES), and the climate models run CLUBB in 5-minute substeps.

code.cite: MOM6 equations of state and freezing point (main, 20 Nov 2026)
code.topic: Ocean model (GFDL, NCAR CESM3) seawater density options
code.note: All eight density options compared with TEOS-10 (GSW) or EOS-80 over temperature, salinity and pressure up to 6000 dbar: differences are the published fitting errors of each formula, the TEOS-10 option matches exactly, and the density derivatives agree with finite differences everywhere. Freezing points agree with TEOS-10. The developers' own documented known bugs (old WRIGHT option, a GSW second-derivative issue) were not counted.

code.topic: Ocean boundary-layer mixing (MOM6, CESM, E3SM MPAS-Ocean)
code.note: Read the core K-profile code against Large, McWilliams & Doney (1994): stability functions, their coefficients and continuity, velocity scales including the pure-convection limit, the shape-function coefficients and the unresolved-shear term all match. Code reviewed and key formulas recomputed, not run in a model.

code.cite: YSU boundary-layer scheme, NCAR MMM-physics (d524bc9, 18 Nov 2026)
code.note: Ran the scheme on 180 test columns (time steps 30–900 s, surface heat flux −50 to 400 W/m², evaporation, winds 0.5–15 m/s): potential temperature and water vapour are conserved to round-off, matching the surface fluxes. The heat tendency is returned as temperature and converted back correctly in the MPAS wrapper.

code.topic: Falling rain and graupel in GFS/UFS (semi-Lagrangian scheme)
code.note: Extracted the sedimentation routine and ran 40,000 random columns (layers 20–1,200 m, fall speeds up to 20 m/s, time steps up to 300 s): mass in the column plus surface precipitation is conserved to about one part in 10⁸ (the tiny minimum-value floor), and no negative values. Unlike the WSM6 routine, whose mass loss others have reported. The rest of the scheme was not checked.

code.cite: Noah-MP land model: snow and soil freezing and melting, soil water budget, canopy radiation (NCAR/noahmp 5a32aaf, 18 Nov 2026; CCPP copy b332cc8)
code.topic: Land surface model (UFS/GFS, WRF, MPAS, HRLDAS)
code.note: Ran the freezing and melting routine on 400,000 random snow and soil states, and the full model for a year at Bondville, Illinois, plus a colder, snowier version of the same year (4,500 steps with layered snow and a spring melt). Energy in the phase-change step is conserved to round-off, and the water balance error is at most 0.002 mm per step. The supercooled soil-water solver agrees with an exact solution to 0.0006 m³/m³. The canopy radiation scheme gave no negative absorption over 4,608 sun, leaf-area and albedo combinations per option. The 2-m temperature issue Noah-MP shares with the GFS surface layer has been sent to the developers.

code.cite: MYNN-EDMF boundary-layer scheme (CCPP physics b332cc8; NCAR MMM-physics d524bc9 for WRF and MPAS; upstream NCAR/MYNN-EDMF 9a35d5d)
code.topic: Planetary boundary layer and shallow-cumulus mixing (HRRR, RRFS, WRF, MPAS)
code.note: Ran 6,000 column steps (surface heat flux −40 to 400 W/m², winds 0.5–15 m/s, with and without the mass-flux plumes) and checked the heat, moisture and momentum budgets. Two errors in the CCPP and WRF/MPAS copies: (1) when negative cloud water from the plume transport is removed, its latent heat is counted twice, creating heat (mean 25 W/m², up to about 900 W/m² in single steps of our cloudy test columns); (2) the surface air density uses T + 0.608q instead of T(1 + 0.608q), so surface heat, moisture and momentum fluxes enter about 1% too strongly in humid air. Both were already fixed in the upstream code by its developers (October and November 2026, versions 6.1.0–6.1.1); the copies in CCPP and MMM-physics have not yet been updated (a WRF update is pending). With the first error corrected and the scheme's deliberate dissipative heating left out, the liquid-water potential temperature budget closes to 0.02 W/m².

code.cite: GFDL fast saturation adjustment, fv_sat_adj (CCPP physics b332cc8)
code.topic: Condensation, freezing and melting inside the FV3 dynamical core (GFS/UFS with GFDL microphysics)
code.note: Ran the adjustment on 20,000 random grid boxes (190–315 K, 150–1,050 hPa, 50–130% relative humidity, all six water species, some small negative values from transport), hydrostatic and non-hydrostatic, intermediate and last steps, with and without the condensate-loading build option. Total water and moist internal energy (with temperature-dependent latent heats) are conserved to round-off in every case; temperature changes up to 8.5 K. Negative cloud ice that cannot be filled from snow is passed on to graupel, which is the routine's documented filling order, not a loss.

code.cite: GFDL cloud microphysics v3 and its coupling to FV3 in the UFS (CCPP physics b332cc8; FV3 dev/emc 0492f16)
code.topic: Cloud microphysics in the UFS suites FV3_GFS_v16_gfdlmpv3 and FV3_HAFS_v1_gfdlmpv3_tedmf
code.note: Ran 2,000 random cloudy columns. Inside the scheme, water is conserved to 10⁻¹⁴ kg/m² and its own dry-energy check passes at 10⁻¹³. But in the physics-suite path the scheme returns humidities relative to the new (dry + vapour) air mass, and the UFS driver multiplies them by the old layer mass, so water species gain or lose mass in proportion to the vapour that condensed or evaporated (up to 0.02–0.03 kg/m² per step in our deliberately supersaturated test columns). The older 2019 version scales its tendencies correctly. This was already found by others: a fix (rescaling by the new/old layer mass) and a second fix for rain falling with the ice heat capacity are in an open pull request to ufs-community/ccpp-physics (#413, October 2026).

code.cite: Zhang–McFarlane deep convection, CAM CCPP version (ESCOMP/atmospheric_physics 0e23c43, 20 Nov 2026): zm_convr, zm_conv_evap, zm_conv_convtran
code.topic: Deep convection in CESM (CAM) and E3SM
code.note: Ran 600 random soundings (tropical ocean, tropical land and cold continental; 264 convecting, rain up to 68 mm/day, surface snow up to 16 mm/day). Water and energy balance to round-off in each step, using CAM's own convention: the convective core balances surface precipitation plus detrained liquid, and the rain-evaporation step balances evaporation and the heat of fusion carried by surface snow. Convective tracer transport conserves tracer mass to 10⁻¹⁷ of the column, for tracers defined on moist or dry air. The momentum transport routine was not tested.

code.cite: Zhang–McFarlane deep convection, E3SM EAM version (E3SM master 9b3897d, 24 Nov 2026): zm_conv_main and zm_conv_evap, with and without convective microphysics
code.topic: Deep convection in E3SM v3 (EAM; also the basis of the EAMxx C++ port)
code.note: Ran 1,800 random soundings (tropical ocean, tropical land, cold continental) in three set-ups: the E3SM v3 default (dCAPE trigger, unrestricted launch level, dynamic closure adjustment and convective microphysics on, with bulk sulfate for droplet and ice nucleation), the same without microphysics, and the base EAM defaults. Rain up to 80 mm/day, snow up to 12 mm/day, detrained ice up to 7.6 mm/day. Water and energy balance to round-off in every case, using E3SM's own energy-checker accounting (precipitation plus reserved liquid, snow plus reserved ice). Tracer and momentum transport were not tested.

code.cite: NOAA GHCN-Monthly v4 production source, including the Pairwise Homogenization Algorithm (NCEI release of 17 Mar 2025)
code.topic: Station temperature homogenization behind NOAAGlobalTemp and GISTEMP
code.note: Read the break detection (SNHT statistic and its critical-value tables), model selection (BIC/AIC, t and F tests with their tables), the Tukey-hinge median of pairwise adjustment estimates, the sort routine, how adjustments are applied segment by segment, and the z-score and spatial-corroboration quality control. All match Menne & Williams (2009) and the published QC. Two known design choices: SNHT critical values are held at the n = 250 value for longer series, and the tests do not allow for autocorrelation; the algorithm relies on confirmation across many station pairs instead. Code reviewed, not built or run; neighbour selection and changepoint merging were not read in detail.

Read the bias, RMSE, seasonal-cycle, spatial-distribution and interannual-variability scores and the weighting of the overall score; they match Collier et al. (2018). One latent inconsistency: for site (point) data, ILAMB 2.7 builds its interannual-variability score from anomalies about the time mean only, so the seasonal cycle is counted as interannual variability, whereas the gridded path removes the annual cycle first. The score is off by default (skip_iav = True) and no shipped configuration turns it on for site data; ilamb3 has no interannual-variability score. Code reviewed, not run.

code.topic: CMIP6 preprocessing and control-run drift removal
code.note: Read the drift removal (linear trend in the parent control run from the branch point, aligned by the CMIP6 branch-time metadata) and the longitude, grid and vertex fixes. A synthetic control run with a known drift, branched into historical and scenario runs, was detrended exactly. With NumPy 2.5 the drift-removal step stops with a TypeError (a date-index type, fixable in one line), which gives no wrong results. Longitude 0 is relabelled 360, which the package handles.

Ran ydrunpctl/eca_tx90p and the etccdi_tx90p operator on a synthetic 60-year AR(1) series with a 1961–1990 base. The eca_* operators have no bootstrap, so the in-base exceedance rate is biased low (9.9% vs 10.6% out of base), the known Zhang et al. (2005) effect; this is documented, and CDO's etccdi_* operators apply the bootstrap, giving 10.6% in base vs 10.6% out of base. ydrunpctl percentiles agree with exact percentiles to within about 0.15 K (0.7 K at the ends of the year). No error found.

code.topic: CIN, LFC/EL choice, mixed-layer and most-unstable parcels, downdraft CAPE
code.note: Read cape_cin, lfc, el, mixed_parcel and downdraft_cape and ran 500 random soundings with capping inversions and mid-level stable layers. CAPE and CIN follow the documented definitions (net area LFC to EL; net area below the LFC, set to zero if positive). One issue: lfc() and el() compute the LCL from the parcel's virtual temperature when called from cape_cin, placing it 13–44 hPa too high. This is already reported, with a fix, in MetPy PR #4067 (May 2026). With that fix, CAPE changed in 52 of 473 soundings by at most 79 J/kg (median 4 J/kg), CIN by at most 12 J/kg. Earlier checks (12 Nov) found surface-based CAPE and the LCL correct.
